title: Admonitio ad astronomos
author: Johannes Kepler
full_title: Admonitio ad astronomos, rerumque coelestium studiosos, de raris mirisque anni 1631 phaenomenis, Veneris puta et Mercurii in Solem incursu
source: Johannes Kepler's notice to astronomers, excerpted from his Ephemeris for 1631 and edited by Jacob Bartsch. First printed at Leipzig in 1629, with Bartsch's dedication to Philipp Müller dated 5/15 October 1629. This is the second printing (Frankfurt: Godefrid Tampach, 1630), to which Bartsch added a new letter to Müller, an address to the reader and the calculations for the two conjunctions.
transcribed_from: the page images of the copy in the Royal Library, Copenhagen (KB 52,94).
summary: Kepler withdraws his claim in the Astronomiae pars optica that Venus could not cross the Sun in this century: the calculation puts a transit of Venus on 6 December 1631 and one of Mercury on 7 November. He asks astronomers, princes and clergy everywhere to prepare telescopes or pinholes and to report what they see, since the size of Venus against the Sun would test his assumptions about the proportions of the planets.

The telescope, first made in the Netherlands (*Belgium* then meant the whole of the Low Countries): Hans Lipperhey of Middelburg applied for a patent on one in October 1608. Galileo built his own the next year and turned it on the sky.
